# BakingSlim

> A single-page buyer's guide to BakingSlim, a once-daily metabolic balance capsule combining chromium picolinate with a 510 mg proprietary botanical blend. Written for readers in the United States at https://bakingslim-us.vercel.app/. Orders complete on the official checkout with BuyGoods as retailer of record. Last reviewed 17 November 2026.

BakingSlim is taken as one capsule daily with a full glass of water. Its Supplement Facts publish exactly two figures: chromium as chromium picolinate at 100 mcg, 286% of the Daily Value, and a Proprietary Metabolic Blend totalling 510 mg. That blend contains eight named botanicals — green tea leaf extract, apple cider vinegar, berberine HCl, ginger root, cinnamon bark extract, bitter orange fruit extract, cayenne fruit and banaba leaf extract — with no individual amount published for any of them. The capsule count per bottle is not published either, and the advertised supply lengths do not reconcile: at one capsule a day the three and six bottle packages imply 30 capsules per bottle, while the two-bottle package implies 15. The seller describes the product as support for cravings, fullness and the body's use of fat for fuel, and states in its own FAQ that it is meant to work alongside healthy eating and movement rather than replace them. Three packages are sold: two bottles at $79 each ($158 plus an unpublished shipping charge), three bottles at $69 each ($207 posted free, about $2.30 a day) and six bottles at $49 each ($294 posted free, about $1.63 a day). Every package carries a 60-day, no-questions-asked money-back guarantee under which bottles do not need to be returned. One payment, no auto-billing. Not for anyone under 18, pregnant or nursing.

## Sources cited on this page

- [NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: dietary supplements for weight loss](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/WeightLoss-Consumer/): reports little scientific evidence that weight-loss supplements work, states that bitter orange might not be safe, and notes that green tea extract has been linked to liver damage in some people.
- [NIDDK: choosing a safe and successful weight-loss program](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/weight-management/choosing-a-safe-successful-weight-loss-program): calls a conversation with a health care professional an important first step, and names results-without-changes claims as a warning sign.
- [MedlinePlus: weight control](https://medlineplus.gov/weightcontrol.html): consumer background on weight management.
- [NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: what you need to know](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/WYNTK-Consumer/): a plain-language primer on what dietary supplements are and how they are regulated.
- [FDA: dietary supplements](https://www.fda.gov/food/dietary-supplements): supplements fall under food law rather than medicines law in the United States, with no approval before sale.
- [FTC: health claims](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/advertising-marketing/health-claims): the advertising rules a supplement health claim has to meet.
- [National Alliance for Eating Disorders](https://www.allianceforeatingdisorders.com/): a free, clinician-staffed helpline, linked for anyone for whom thoughts about food or weight have become distressing.
